definition: A dense granite rock polished with a concave running band, delivered down the sheet toward the house.
The circular scoring target painted beneath the ice at each end, comprising concentric coloured rings and the button.
The prepared, pebbled ice playing surface bounded by hog lines, tee lines, and backboards.
The traditional sweeping implement historically made of corn straw, now replaced by modern synthetic brushes.
A modern sweeping device with an adjustable synthetic fabric head used to control stone distance and curl.
A stone intentionally positioned in front of the house to shield counting stones or protect delivery lanes.
Deliveries thrown with calibrated momentum designed to come to rest gently inside the house.
To brush the ice vigorously before a moving stone to reduce friction, maintain velocity, and hold a straighter line.
The smooth, balanced glide out from the hack executed on a low-friction Teflon or stainless steel slider.
A stone that marginally touches the outer perimeter of the twelve-foot circle to qualify as a potential counting rock.
The rubber-lined foot supports anchored in the ice from which curlers push off to deliver stones.
Airborne moisture freezing onto the pebbled sheet that increases drag and causes erratic stone deceleration.
The common name for curling stones traditionally crafted from durable microgranite quarried on Ailsa Craig.
A shot that strikes a stationary guard to propel both it and the delivered stone into scoring positions.
A delivered stone thrown with greater velocity and momentum than requested by the skip's broom call.
Lightly sweeping directly ahead of a stone to remove loose ice crumbs and debris without altering line.
A defensive tactical success in which the opponent holding the hammer is limited to scoring only a single point.
Scoring one or more points in an end without having the advantage of the last-stone hammer.
The balanced forward motion of a delivering curler riding the slider smoothly down the centre line.
The lateral curved arc a rotating stone traces across the pebble as it travels toward the target.
A sudden-death tiebreaker end contested when the match score remains deadlocked after regulation play.
The delivery trajectories and visual paths toward the broom designated by the skip in the house.
High-velocity takeout deliveries designed to strike an opponent stone and roll both rocks completely out of play.
A grooved or heavily swept path on the sheet where delivered stones tend to follow a consistent run.
The wooden bumper or padded perimeter structure enclosing the ice sheet behind each hack.
The rotational handles applied to the stone at release, categorized as either an in-turn or out-turn.
The sequence of sixteen stones delivered alternately by two opposing teams throughout each end.
The precise geometric alignment needed on carom, hit-and-roll, and promotion deliveries.
A stone thrown with insufficient weight that stalls and stops well short of the skip's intended target.
Delicate carom shots that glance lightly off the edge of a stationary rock to redirect toward the house.
A sudden, sharp increase in lateral curl that occurs as a decelerating stone expends its forward momentum.
The precision-machined inner and outer contact borders defining the stone's circular running band.
The concentric coloured four-foot, eight-foot, and twelve-foot circles that make up the house.
The pace of the ice sheet, calibrated in seconds required for a stone to travel from hog line to tee line.
The replaceable sweeping components featuring specialized fabric and foam padding mounted on brush handles.
A formal competitive game between two teams contested over a regulation schedule of eight or ten ends.
The progressive tally of points earned by counting stones across completed ends of play.
The official game timer displaying each team's allotted strategic thinking time during a match.
A concise tactical conference held between ends or during a timeout to align strategy and read sheet conditions.
The Scottish island of Ailsa Craig, renowned globally as the primary source of premium curling stone granite.
Canada's historic national men's curling championship tournament, inaugurated in 1927.
Jennifer Jones, legendary Canadian skip who captured Olympic gold and six national Scotties titles.
Rachel Homan, elite world champion skip and multi-time Canadian national women's champion.
Bruce Mouat, world champion skip and Olympic silver medalist who directs Scotland's top men's team.
The historic long-term sponsor name indelibly linked with the Canadian women's national Scotties tournament.
A scoring unit awarded for each stone resting closer to the tee than any stone delivered by the opposing team.
The lead player who opens the end by throwing the team's initial two stones and establishing early positioning.
The vice-skip who delivers the fifth and sixth stones and takes over house strategy when the skip delivers.
The mandatory throwing lineup of four players registered prior to the start of a competitive game.
The physical act of initiating the push from the hack, sliding forward, and cleanly releasing the stone.
The stationary posture or delivery stance used by stick curlers delivering rocks without sliding from the hack.
An adaptive delivery cue attached to the stone handle, permitted in wheelchair and stick curling disciplines.
Adaptive mobility equipment used by wheelchair curlers who deliver stones from a stationary position without sweeping.
A specialized thermal instrument used by ice technicians to monitor ice and subfloor brine temperatures.
An end that concludes with no stones in the house, allowing the team that delivered last to retain the hammer.
Keen, fast ice characterized by minimal surface friction that yields extended stone travel with little effort.
A promotion shot that strikes a stationary guard stone and advances it directly forward into the scoring house.
Purified deionized liquid applied across the sheet through specialized nozzles to form uniform ice pebbles.
Thin takeout shots designed to graze just enough of an opponent guard to remove it while preserving line.
The predictable sideways deflection of a delivering rock after striking an opponent stone.
A subtle, controlled wrist motion used upon release to apply positive, uniform handle rotation.
A stone illegally contacted by a player's body, shoe, or equipment while in motion along the sheet.
The mechanical refrigeration process that circulates coolant beneath the floor to maintain consistent ice hardness.
The true horizontal plane required across competition sheets to eliminate side-to-side drift or fall.
The skip's visual alignment down the sheet when positioning the broom target for the delivering player.
A high-precision optical device utilized by tournament umpires to determine which stone lies closest to the pin.
The subtle slope, fall, or crown across an ice sheet that alters the natural draw path of rotating stones.
Delivering a stone with firm, forceful takeout weight to blast through guards and clear the house.
The certified synthetic woven fabric stretched over tournament brush heads to sweep competition ice.
Shed areas where the ice lacks standard lateral curl, causing stones to run exceptionally straight.
An accredited technical official or digital system managing thinking-time clocks for both competing teams.
The refined sensory feel and weight control a curler relies on to throw precise draw weight consistently.
The natural deceleration exerted on a traveling stone as it contacts ice pebble and gradually expends momentum.
A traditional four-person curling discipline contested with alternating female and male athletes.
The front-end duo of lead and second whose tactical duties include setting early rocks and heavy sweeping.
Fragile surface frost accumulation on the pebble tops caused by elevated humidity inside the ice shed.
The effortless forward glide of a stone traversing an exceptionally keen and clean section of ice.
High-traction rubber slip-on footwear worn over shoes to provide secure footing on slippery ice.
A tight cluster of several stones gathered closely inside the four-foot ring or directly on the button.
The razor-sharp nickel or steel cutting edge mounted on an ice scraper used to plane high spots from the sheet.
The official World Curling certification emblem printed on approved tournament brush heads and fabrics.
A skip's tactical command directing the delivering curler to aim outside the standard broom line.
A brisk, cold shed temperature that preserves pebble integrity and keeps stone travel crisp.
Precision shaving of the ice sheet with a motorized scraper to eliminate ridges and create a flat playing field.
The vertical rotational axis around which a stone spins upon its hollowed circular running band.
A delivery thrown with deficient weight that stalls and stops well ahead of the desired target zone.
The rear portion of curling sliders where balance and body weight are centred during the slide.
Arena spectators who maintain quiet during delivery out of respect and cheer following great shot execution.
Units of four athletes, or pairs in mixed doubles, working cooperatively through delivery and sweeping.
The codified international laws established by World Curling governing fair play, equipment, and scoring.
A sanctioned bonspiel, tour competition, or championship staging multiple draws across several days.
The presiding committee of umpires and chief technical delegates supervising tournament competition.
The team captains who orchestrate strategy, signal shot choices from the house, and throw final stones.
The front-end players who open each end by establishing corner guards, centre guards, or early draws.
A delivery infraction, such as failing to release the handle before crossing the near hog line.
The offensive strategy of accumulating multiple stones in the rings to produce a multi-point score.
Specific strategic areas on the sheet, notably the house and the Free Guard Zone between tee and hog line.
The trophy, championship banner, medals, or purse awarded to the winning team at a major bonspiel.
The repeated delivery tracks along the ice that become polished and keen through continuous sweeping and travel.
Executing a shot with calibrated line and weight to park a stone precisely in a designated tactical spot.
The tactical placement option available once per game to each team in mixed doubles discipline play.
Curling facilities housing multiple sheets, or the historic Scottish term identifying curling teams.
The specialized, climate-controlled arena buildings that house indoor curling sheets and refrigeration plants.
The historic innovators in Scotland who formalized curling rules, stones, and clubs during the early modern era.
A scheduled draw or preliminary stage of pool competition within a comprehensive tournament format.
Tournament ranking placements that determine bracket positions and draw schedules for championship playoffs.
Group divisions in round-robin tournaments where teams contest preliminary matches to earn playoff berths.
Verbal decisions and commands issued by the skip regarding weight calibration, ice line, and sweeping.
Shot-making percentage evaluations compiled by official scorers to measure individual and team efficiency.
Numerical grades assigned by statistical judges to quantify shot execution success on a zero-to-four scale.
The cumulative aggregate score of counting stones tallied across all completed ends of a curling match.
An accredited competition official who inspects equipment, monitors hog lines, and resolves rule disputes.
Respectful audience applause acknowledging superb shotmaking, traditionally withheld until the shot is complete.
The traditional post-game handshake shared between opposing curlers alongside the greeting 'Good curling'.
The championship honor and trophy awarded to the victorious team concluding a season-long competition.
